label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
reason: formatting, assistant talk or a placeholder
output:
Here's a draft. I wrote it to be read out loud, since Denise will be the one reading it, so the sentences are meant to be easy to say. Where it says [name], put in whatever Nana calls you.

---

Dear Nana,

Denise is reading this to you, so Denise, hi, please do the voices.

I'm so sorry I can't be there tonight. I'm on call all week and I tried to find someone to swap with me and couldn't. Everyone keeps telling me it's fine, and I know it is, but I'm still sitting here in Toronto wishing I was at that kitchen table with you. So this is the next best thing. You're stuck listening to me, and you can't interrupt.

I wanted to write you a proper letter because you deserve more than a card. Also because a card has about four lines and I have a lot more than four lines.

Fifty-one years on Kathleen Street. I've been trying to wrap my head around that number. You moved in and raised half the family in that kitchen, and honestly I think the house is a little bit you. Everything I remember about it is tied up with you. The summers, mostly. You let me stay up to watch the Expos and the Jays on that tiny TV on the counter, as long as I dried the dishes first. I thought I was getting away with something. Looking back, I think you just figured out the cheapest way to get a kid to do dishes. It worked, by the way. I'd have dried dishes for a week to see one more inning.

And the back steps. You out there at six in the morning with your tea, and me coming out half asleep, and you would not say one word until that cup was empty. I used to think you were just grumpy before breakfast. I know now that it was the best part of your day, and you let me sit there in it with you. I don't think I've ever felt as calm as I did on those steps. I still try to find that feeling and I never quite do.

Then there's crib. You taught me when I was about seven, and in all the years since, you never once let me win. Not once. Not when I was little, not when I was clearly crushed about it. I'm grateful now, because it meant that when I finally did beat you, it counted. And when I skunked you for the first time, I was fifteen and I was absolutely unbearable about it, and you went and made me a whole pan of butter tarts. I've thought about that a lot. Most people would have flipped the board. You baked. That is the most gracious losing in the history of the game, and I'm not sure I've ever deserved it.

You've also been looking after me from a distance for a long time. When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me a twenty-dollar bill taped inside a card that said it was "for pizza, you look thin on the computer." I want you to know I did buy the pizza. I'm not saying that was the only reason, but I felt watched in the best way. Nobody else on earth has ever looked at me through a video call and decided I needed feeding.

And then last Christmas, when my pager went off in the middle of dinner and everybody at the table went quiet, you asked whether the internet was broken again and whether I'd fixed it. I've been trying to explain my job to people for ten years, and you summed it up better than I ever have. Now you ask me every single time I'm on call, "Did anything break?" I love that more than I can say. So for the record, this week something probably will break, and I'll fix it, and I'll be thinking about you while I do.

Now, the part I most want to say. I'm proud of you. You're eighty-eight years old and you looked at the house you've lived in for over half a century and decided it was time. Nobody made you. Nobody talked you into it. You picked Elmwood Terrace yourself, you looked at the options, and you chose. That takes a kind of nerve I'm not sure I have, and I'm fifty-four years younger than you. I hope you know how many people in this family are going to look at what you did and think, "Okay, that's how you do it."

I also think the place looks great. Second floor, and your window looks out on the parking lot and that big maple. It'll be bare this time of year, but come spring it's going to be something. I'm already picturing you with your tea in the morning, not saying a word until the cup is done, just with a better view than most of us get. You'll have a new set of back steps, they just happen to be a window.

And I heard the news, so I'll say it. They have a crib league. A crib league! Nana, I want you to take a moment to feel sorry for those people. They have no idea what's coming. They think they signed up for a friendly game on a Tuesday, and meanwhile you've been running the church ladies for years. Be kind to them. Maybe let one of them win. Actually, no. Don't. You never let me, so nobody gets special treatment.

I won't pretend leaving the house isn't a big thing. It is. That kitchen has been the middle of a lot of lives, mine included, and it's okay to feel that tonight, and to cry a little if you want. I'm probably going to, a bit, wherever I am. But it was never really the walls. It was you, and the people you fed and talked to and beat at cards in there. All of that comes with you. Every bit of it fits in a second-floor room with a view of a maple tree. You're taking the house with you, Nana. You always were the house.

Denise has the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, which means the best things are going to good hands. I asked for the crib board, and I hope that's all right. It seemed like the one thing that should stay in play.

So here's the plan. I'm coming up the weekend of December 5th, as soon as this rotation is over. Come hell or high water, or a broken server, I'll be there. I'll bring the board. We'll set it up at your new place, and you'll deal, and it'll be the first game at Elmwood. I'm going to try my hardest to win, and I fully expect you not to let me.

Get some sleep tonight, Nana. Have your tea on the steps tomorrow morning, one last time, and take your time with it.

I love you so much. See you on the 5th.

[name]

---

A few notes:

- It comes to roughly 1,200 words, so about 8 to 9 minutes read aloud. Easy to trim if you want it shorter.
- The "fifty-four years younger" line is 88 minus your 34. Cut it if you'd rather not do the math in front of her.
- I put the "Denise, please do the voices" line at the top to give Denise an easy way in, and to get the first laugh early, before anyone's eyes are wet. Cut it if it doesn't feel like her.
- The line about the maple being bare is a guess for November. If it's wrong, change it.
- If any line sounds like something you wouldn't say, swap in your own words. It'll land better in your voice than in mine.
